analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share vehicle repair data and tools with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 56 cosponsors split evenly between the parties and cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never took it up and it died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars are computers on wheels, and manufacturers increasingly control the diagnostic data and software needed to fix them. This bill would have barred carmakers from blocking owners or independent repair shops from accessing vehicle-generated repair data and repair tools, required a standardized, secure way to get that data directly from the vehicle, and stopped manufacturers from forcing the use of their own brand of parts outside of recall and warranty work. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce these rules, and safety regulators would set standards for secure data access.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners and lessees, who could choose any repair shop or fix their own cars without paying dealer prices; independent repair shops and aftermarket parts makers, who could compete for repair work on equal footing; and used-car buyers, since competitive repair keeps older cars on the road cheaper.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers could not use technological or contractual barriers to stop owners or their chosen repair shops from accessing vehicle-generated data on diagnostics, repair, and calibration [S3].

Repair data, tools, schematics, and software had to be made available to owners, independent shops, and aftermarket parts makers at fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory cost, with no fees, licenses, or mandated decryption devices [S3].

Outside of recall and warranty repairs, manufacturers could not mandate or imply a mandate to use their own brand of parts, tools, or equipment, and had to add a prominent notice that owners can choose their own parts [S3].

If a manufacturer transmits vehicle data wirelessly, it had to make that data available directly to owners and their designees through a standardized access platform, with security standards set by the safety regulator and the platform run by an entity independent of the manufacturers [S3].
Contracts that try to waive these rights — for example, requiring owners to give up their right to choose a repair shop as a condition of warranty service — would be void [S3].
The FTC could enforce violations the same way it enforces unfair or deceptive practices, with a complaint process open to any person [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, who would lose their near-monopoly on diagnostic data, software locks, and dealer service revenue, and would bear the cost of building and securing standardized data access. Dealership service departments would face more competition. Some compliance costs could be passed into vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Cybersecurity and privacy: opening vehicle data to outside parties can create new pathways for hacking or theft; the bill acknowledges this by allowing manufacturers to keep cryptographic protections and requiring federal security standards before the wireless platform goes live [S3].

Preemption: the bill would override any state law that mandates use of a particular brand of parts, tools, or equipment, which could weaken stronger state right-to-repair rules, and it preempts state duties narrower than the federal ones [S3].

The standardized access platform would be run by an entity composed of industry stakeholders, including the manufacturers themselves, raising the question of whether the gatekeeper would act in owners' interests [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the compliance cost: manufacturers must build secure, standardized data access and share repair information they currently control, costs that could show up in vehicle prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and everyday: competitive repair prices, freedom to pick your own shop, and longer life for the cars most families depend on. The risks are real but addressed in the bill's design — security standards come before wireless data access opens, and manufacturers keep the ability to secure safety-critical systems. The weakest point is industry's role on the access-platform board. On balance, the bill transfers control over repair from manufacturers back to the people who own the vehicles.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2023 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; a subcommittee approved it by voice vote in November 2023, but the full committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced February 9, 2023 by Rep. Neal Dunn with three original cosponsors across both parties, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
It gathered 56 cosponsors, split exactly evenly — 28 Democrats and 28 Republicans — making it one of the more bipartisan bills of the Congress [S4].
On November 2, 2023, the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never took up the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep their control over vehicle repair data, software, and the service revenue that comes with it. Independent repair shops and car owners got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, not car owners or repair shops

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 28 Democratic and 28 Republican cosponsors plus a Republican lead sponsor and bipartisan original cosponsors — but the committee chair and House leadership, both Republicans, never advanced it.

industries.note: They would lose control of diagnostic data, repair software, and parts mandates that steer owners to dealers, and the service revenue that comes with it. Their interest in keeping that control runs directly against owners' freedom to repair cheaply.
Guaranteed access to repair data, tools, and fair-priced information would let them compete for modern-vehicle repair work they are increasingly locked out of. Their gain is owners' savings.
The bill bars manufacturers from blocking compatible aftermarket parts and from mandating their own brand, expanding the market for independent parts makers.
Dealer service centers would face more competition from independent shops as repair data and parts choice open up, though they keep recall and warranty work.
Insurers would gain a seat on the FTC advisory committee and could benefit from cheaper, faster repairs, but they also face new data-access dynamics for claims and telematics.
